newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon government raises fears of election delay.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon government raises fears of election delay.

text.p: The government withdrew a bill amending Lebanon's municipal elections law, arousing concern among politicians and the media that it may be planning to delay the country's first local elections in 34 years.

Newspapers said some members of the pro-Syrian government were worried about the vote, partly because almost all Christian opposition groups had decided to participate -- ending an electoral boycott that many disgruntled Lebanese Christians have maintained since the 1975-90 civil war.

The vote for mayors and local councils, scheduled for June, would be Lebanon's first local elections since 1963 and holding them is widely considered a test of the government's democratic convictions.

However, billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri withdrew the bill from parliament late on Thursday, saying revisions were needed on several issues, including voting arrangements for people still unable to return to villages they fled during the war.
It was not clear if the government would now be able to meet the June schedule.

However, Hariri could face problems since President Elias Hrawi, a Maronite Christian, has made clear he opposes a delay and three ministers loyal to him voted on Thursday against withdrawing the bill from parliament.
Newspapers quoted sources close to Hrawi as saying a delay would demoralise voters and damage the state's credibility.

The dispute was Lebanon's second elections-related crisis in two days following Thursday's resignation of the head of the constitutional council in protest at political pressures over appeals against the results of last year's parliamentary polls.

The council is considering 18 appeals to overturn the results of individual races on grounds of intimidation by the authorities and other abuses, and one claim for cancellation of the entire election.

Judge Wajdi al-Mallat, 74, a respected Maronite jurist, resigned without explanation days before the council was due to announce its decisions, and newspapers said a second member of the 10-judge tribunal was also considering resigning.

"Mallat's resignation has caused deep shock in Lebanese society," the left-wing Beirut newspaper as-Safir said on Friday. "It has dealt a severe blow to people's hopes in their institutions as well as in their democratic system."

The newspaper quoted Mallat as complaining that he wanted the council to be a court with international standards but politicians pressuring it wanted it to be like other judicial institutions in Lebanon which commanded little confidence.
